title: Core ML
summary: Apple's on-device ML framework: run models on iPhone/Mac with the Neural Engine.
details: Core ML deploys models on Apple devices, executing on the Neural Engine, GPU, or CPU via a unified API. Models convert from PyTorch/TensorFlow with coremltools, and iOS 17+ supports transformer architectures natively. It powers on-device Siri, camera features, and third-party apps — with privacy as the pitch: data never leaves the device.
min_requirements: iOS 15+ for transformers; Neural Engine recommended

demo.title: Convert with coremltools
demo.program:
import torch, coremltools as ct
model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(10, 2)).eval()
traced = torch.jit.trace(model, torch.randn(1, 10))
mlmodel = ct.convert(traced, inputs=[ct.TensorType(shape=(1, 10))])
print("converted:", type(mlmodel).__name__)

title: TensorFlow Lite
summary: Google's mobile inference runtime: small, fast models on Android, iOS, and microcontrollers.
details: TensorFlow Lite runs quantized and pruned models on phones and embedded devices with delegates for GPU (Metal/OpenGL), NNAPI, and Hexagon DSP. The TFLite converter applies post-training quantization and operator fusion; the Model Maker simplifies retraining. It remains the default for Android on-device ML and TinyML on microcontrollers.

demo.title: Convert to TFLite with quantization
demo.program:
import tensorflow as tf
model = tf.keras.Sequential([tf.keras.layers.Dense(2, input_shape=(10,))])
conv = tf.lite.TFLiteConverter.from_keras_model(model)
conv.optimizations = [tf.lite.Optimize.DEFAULT]
tflite = conv.convert()
print("tflite bytes:", len(tflite))

title: ONNX Runtime Mobile
summary: Run ONNX models on phones with hardware accelerators via execution providers.
details: ONNX Runtime Mobile executes ONNX models on iOS/Android, dispatching to Core ML, NNAPI, or GPU execution providers for acceleration. Export from PyTorch via torch.onnx, optimize (quantize, fuse), and ship one model file across platforms. It is the cross-platform answer when you cannot commit to a single vendor stack.

demo.title: Export PyTorch to ONNX
demo.program:
import torch
model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(10, 2)).eval()
torch.onnx.export(model, torch.randn(1, 10), "/tmp/m.onnx",
                  input_names=["x"], output_names=["y"],
                  dynamo=False)
print("exported /tmp/m.onnx")

title: llama.cpp
summary: Run LLMs on anything: CPU-first inference with GGUF quantization, from servers to phones.
details: llama.cpp is a C/C++ inference engine running quantized LLMs on CPUs, GPUs (CUDA/Metal/Vulkan), and mobile chips with no heavy dependencies. GGUF quants (Q4_K_M etc.) shrink 70B models to ~40GB; Metal and CUDA backends offload layers to GPU. It powers Ollama, LM Studio, and countless local-AI apps — the engine behind the local LLM revolution.

demo.title: Run a model with llama.cpp
demo.program:
llama-cli -m model-q4k.gguf -p "Explain gravity simply." -n 128
# server mode: llama-server -m model-q4k.gguf --port 8080

title: MLC LLM
summary: Compile LLMs to native code for phones, browsers, and GPUs via Apache TVM.
details: MLC LLM (Machine Learning Compilation) uses Apache TVM to compile models into optimized native libraries for iOS, Android, WebGPU, CUDA, and more — with 4-bit quantization built in. The same model compiles to a phone app, a browser demo, or a GPU server. It is the 'write once, run anywhere fast' path for local LLMs.

demo.title: Compile a model with MLC LLM
demo.program:
mlc_llm gen_config --model Llama-3-8B --quantization q4f16_1 \
  --conv-template llama-3 -o dist/
# then build the lib for your target (iphone/android/webgpu)

title: ExecuTorch
summary: Meta's on-device runtime for PyTorch models: from research model to phone app.
details: ExecuTorch (Meta/PyTorch) takes PyTorch models (via Export) and runs them on mobile and embedded devices with delegate backends (Core ML, NPU, DSP). It unifies the path from training in PyTorch to deployment on device — no framework rewrite. Powers Meta's on-device AI features and is fully open-source.

demo.title: Export for ExecuTorch
demo.program:
import torch
from executorch import exir
model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(10, 2)).eval()
prog = exir.to_edge(exir.capture(model, (torch.randn(1, 10),)))
print("edge program dialects:", list(prog.exported_program().dialects))

title: INT8 Quantization
summary: Shrink models 4x with 8-bit weights/activations — the workhorse of mobile deployment.
details: INT8 post-training quantization converts weights (and optionally activations) to 8-bit integers with per-channel scales, cutting model size 4x and speeding mobile CPUs/DSPs that have INT8 units. Calibration on representative data preserves accuracy; quantization-aware training recovers the last points. Nearly every shipped mobile model uses it.

demo.title: INT8 scale math
demo.program:
import torch
w = torch.randn(1000)
scale = w.abs().max() / 127
q = torch.round(w / scale).clamp(-128, 127)
print("max abs error:", float((w - q*scale).abs().max()))

title: INT4 / GGUF Quantization
summary: 4-bit weights for LLMs on phones: 7B models in ~4GB of RAM.
details: INT4 quantization (GPTQ/AWQ-style, GGUF K-quants) compresses LLM weights to 4 bits with grouped scales, fitting 7-8B models in ~4-5GB — phone territory. Quality loss is small at 7B+ scales. Combined with llama.cpp or MLC, it is what makes capable chatbots run fully offline on flagship phones.

demo.title: Check GGUF size
demo.program:
ls -lh *Q4_K_M.gguf
# 7B Q4_K_M ~= 4.1GB; 70B Q4_K_M ~= 39GB

title: Model Pruning for Mobile
summary: Remove unimportant weights before shipping — smaller models, same accuracy.
details: Pruning deletes low-magnitude or low-importance weights (unstructured) or whole channels (structured, mobile-friendly) then fine-tunes to recover accuracy. Structured pruning keeps dense math (fast on mobile); 30-50% sparsity is typical without quality loss. Often combined with quantization for compound compression.

demo.title: Channel pruning sketch
demo.program:
import torch
w = torch.randn(64, 128)  # 64 output channels
importance = w.abs().mean(1)
keep = torch.topk(importance, 48).indices
print(f"pruned {64-48}/64 channels ({(64-48)/64:.0%})")

title: Core ML Tools Conversion
summary: The bridge from PyTorch/TensorFlow to Core ML with optimization passes.
details: coremltools converts traced PyTorch, TF, and ONNX models to Core ML, applying graph passes (fusion, quantization, compute-unit placement). iOS 15+ converters handle transformers; compression utilities do post-training quantization. It is the mandatory toll road for Apple deployment.

demo.title: Conversion options
demo.program:
import coremltools as ct
print("compute units:", ct.ComputeUnit.CPU_AND_GPU, ct.ComputeUnit.ALL)

title: NNAPI Delegates
summary: Android's neural API: route ops to the phone's NPU/DSP/GPU automatically.
details: NNAPI (Android Neural Networks API) lets runtimes (TFLite, ONNX RT) delegate subgraphs to the device's AI accelerators — NPUs, DSPs, GPUs — via vendor drivers. The delegate partitions the graph: supported ops go to hardware, the rest falls back to CPU. Performance varies wildly by device, so real apps benchmark per-device allowlists.

demo.title: Delegate allowlist
demo.program:
allowlist = ["pixel_8", "galaxy_s24"]
device = "pixel_8"
print("use NNAPI:" , device in allowlist)

title: GPU Delegates (TFLite)
summary: Run TFLite models on the phone GPU via Metal/OpenGL/Vulkan delegates.
details: TFLite GPU delegates execute models on mobile GPUs (Metal on iOS, OpenGL/Vulkan on Android), often 2-5x faster than CPU for vision models. Quantized models may fall back where GPU INT8 support is weak — the delegate/quantization interaction is the classic mobile gotcha. Benchmark both paths per model.

demo.title: Delegate selection
demo.program:
backends = {"cpu": 45, "gpu": 12}  # ms per inference
best = min(backends, key=backends.get)
print("fastest:", best, backends[best], "ms")

title: Apple Neural Engine
summary: The 35-TOPS (M4) AI core in every modern Apple device — Core ML's fast lane.
details: The Neural Engine (ANE) is Apple's dedicated ML accelerator: 18 TOPS in M3, 38 in M4, executing Core ML graphs at high efficiency. Models must use ANE-supported ops to benefit; transformers run well on recent OS versions. For Apple deployment, ANE placement is the difference between 'runs' and 'flies'.

demo.title: ANE op support check

title: Qualcomm Hexagon DSP
summary: The AI accelerator in Snapdragon phones — TFLite/ONNX delegate target.
details: Qualcomm's Hexagon DSP/NPU (with the AI Engine) accelerates INT8 models on Snapdragon devices via delegates. The QNN SDK is Qualcomm's native path; TFLite and ONNX Runtime delegate to it. Hundreds of millions of phones carry Hexagon — it is the largest mobile AI accelerator install base.

demo.title: Install base math
demo.program: print("Snapdragon ships ~700M+ units/year with Hexagon AI")

title: Android AICore
summary: Google's on-device Gemini: system-level AI on Pixel with Gemini Nano.
details: Android AICore is Google's system service exposing Gemini Nano (on-device) to apps via the AICore API — summarization, smart reply, and image description without app-bundled models. It handles model updates and safety at the OS level. Available on Pixel 8+ and expanding; the pattern (OS-provided foundation model) is the future of mobile AI APIs.

demo.title: AICore API sketch
demo.program: print("AiCoreService.summarize(text)  # system handles the model")

title: MediaPipe Tasks
summary: Google's cross-platform vision/text/audio task APIs for mobile.
details: MediaPipe Tasks provides ready-made on-device solutions — object detection, face landmarks, gesture recognition, text classification, LLM inference — as simple APIs on Android/iOS/web, with model customization via Model Maker. It is the fastest path from idea to on-device AI feature without ML expertise.

demo.title: Task options
demo.program:
tasks = ["object_detection", "text_classifier", "llm_inference", "gesture"]
print("available:", tasks)

title: whisper.cpp
summary: OpenAI Whisper speech recognition running fully offline on phones and laptops.
details: whisper.cpp ports Whisper to C/C++ with quantized models (tiny to large-v3), running real-time transcription on CPUs — including phones. Core ML and GPU backends accelerate Apple/PC targets. It made private, offline speech recognition a solved problem for apps.
min_requirements: Phone CPU for tiny/base; laptop for small+

demo.title: Transcribe offline
demo.program: ./main -m models/ggml-base.en.bin -f audio.wav --language en

title: Stable Diffusion On-Device
summary: Text-to-image on phones: quantized diffusion with step distillation.
details: On-device Stable Diffusion uses INT8-quantized UNet/text-encoder plus step-distilled samplers (LCM, Turbo) to generate 512px images in seconds on flagship phones (Core ML on iOS, NNAPI/GPU on Android). Apps ship it for private, offline generation — no server, no queue.

demo.title: Step budget
demo.program:
steps, sec_per_step = 4, 0.8  # LCM distilled
print(f"generation: {steps*sec_per_step:.1f}s on-device")

title: Federated Learning Basics
summary: Train across phones without collecting their data — gradients, not records, leave the device.
details: Federated learning trains a shared model by aggregating on-device updates (FedAvg) — raw data never leaves phones. Google's Gboard trains next-word prediction this way. Challenges: heterogeneous devices, communication cost, and privacy attacks on updates (mitigated with secure aggregation + differential privacy). The pattern for privacy-sensitive mobile AI.

demo.title: FedAvg sketch
demo.program:
import torch
clients = [torch.randn(10) for _ in range(5)]
global_w = sum(clients) / len(clients)
print("aggregated update norm:", round(float(global_w.norm()), 3))

title: Mobile Distillation
summary: Distill server models into phone-sized students — the standard mobile-model recipe.
details: Mobile distillation trains small students (MobileBERT, TinyLlama-class, DistilWhisper) from large teachers with mobile-friendly architectures (bottlenecks, fewer layers). The recipe: distill, quantize, benchmark on-device. Most shipped mobile AI features are distilled models — the teacher never leaves the datacenter.

demo.title: Student size target
demo.program:
teacher_mb, ratio = 13000, 40
print(f"student target: ~{teacher_mb//ratio}MB")

title: MLPerf Mobile Benchmarks
summary: The industry scoreboard for on-device AI: latency, accuracy, and power per task.
details: MLPerf Mobile benchmarks image classification, detection, language, and super-resolution on phones, measuring latency and accuracy (power optional). It is how vendors prove NPU claims and how developers compare devices. Submitting requires the closed-division harness; the open division welcomes custom stacks.

demo.title: Scorecard
demo.program:
scores = {"classification_ms": 8.2, "detection_ms": 24.5}
print("lower is better:", scores)

title: Thermal / Power Constraints
summary: Phones throttle: design AI features for sustained performance, not peak benchmarks.
details: Mobile SoCs throttle under sustained load — a model benchmarking 30 tok/s may settle at 12 tok/s after a minute. Thermal/power design means: burst-friendly scheduling, efficiency (tokens/joule) as a metric, and graceful degradation. Ship for the throttled steady state, not the cold benchmark.

demo.title: Throttled throughput
demo.program:
peak, sustained = 30, 12
print(f"design for {sustained} tok/s sustained, not {peak} peak")

title: App-Size Budgets
summary: Every MB of model is MBs of app download — budget ruthlessly.
details: App stores and users punish large downloads: models compete with the rest of the app for a size budget (often 50-200MB total). Tactics: download models on demand, quantize aggressively, share one backbone across features, and stream weights. The size budget is a product constraint, not just engineering.

demo.title: Size budget

title: Knowledge Distillation to Small Models
summary: The full pipeline: teacher to student to quantized phone model.
details: End-to-end small-model pipeline: pick a teacher, distill to a mobile architecture, fine-tune on task data, quantize to INT8/INT4, benchmark on target devices, and ship with on-demand download. This record is the checklist version of the pipeline every on-device team runs.

demo.title: Pipeline checklist
demo.program:
steps = ["distill", "task_finetune", "quantize", "benchmark", "ship"]
print(" -> ".join(steps))

title: Private Cloud Compute
summary: Apple's private AI cloud: scale beyond the device without exposing data.
details: Private Cloud Compute extends Apple Intelligence: requests that need more than on-device models go to Apple-silicon servers with cryptographic guarantees — data is never stored, never accessible to Apple, verifiable by researchers. The pattern (on-device first, private cloud second) is the emerging trust model for personal AI.

demo.title: Routing decision
demo.program:
fits_on_device = False
print("route to:", "on-device" if fits_on_device else "Private Cloud Compute")
